doc.headline: Atlas-L scores {price.atlas-m.atlas-l.overall.gain|abs} points higher than Atlas-M on overall quality at {cost.gap.atlas-l.atlas-m.multiple} its cost; Brisk-S and Open-70B cost less but lapse on policy behaviours.
doc.lede: Atlas-M is not told apart from Atlas-L on any behaviour judged pass or fail, while the cheaper two trail it by up to {compare.atlas-m.brisk-s.declines.task.specul.difference|abs} points on declining speculation and confirming account changes. Nothing declared what a point of quality is worth; above {price.atlas-m.atlas-l.overall.per_point_high_unpaired} per thousand conversations, Atlas-L is the better buy.

caveats.material_if: Only if the owner would accept the cheaper models' policy lapses, or values a point of overall quality above {price.atlas-m.atlas-l.overall.per_point_low_unpaired} per thousand conversations; either moves the pick off Atlas-M.

Only if pairing the arms on their shared cases would undo a separation; every gap here is read as if the arms ran different cases, which reads wider than paired, so pairing would narrow intervals rather than reverse a direction.

Only if a fresh run read Atlas-M's policy rates below Atlas-L's; a lead picked from several candidates tends to shrink on re-run, which would weaken Atlas-L's case for its extra cost, not strengthen it.

decision.text: Atlas-L scores {price.atlas-m.atlas-l.overall.gain|abs} points higher than Atlas-M on overall quality for {price.atlas-m.atlas-l.overall.cost_gap|abs} more per thousand conversations. Brisk-S and Open-70B cost less still, but decline speculation, confirm account changes and avoid unsupported claims less often than either Atlas model.

A point of overall quality worth more than {price.atlas-m.atlas-l.overall.per_point_high_unpaired} per thousand conversations favours Atlas-L; worth less than {price.atlas-m.atlas-l.overall.per_point_low_unpaired}, Atlas-M. Between the two, this run does not settle it.

Ours, not a declared rule: Atlas-M, while a point of overall quality is worth less than {price.atlas-m.atlas-l.overall.per_point_low_unpaired} per thousand conversations and the cheaper models' policy lapses are not acceptable. It holds every policy behaviour at Atlas-L's level for {cost.gap.atlas-l.atlas-m.per_1k|abs} less per thousand conversations. The concierge owner makes the call.

Atlas-M's widest shortfall on overall quality is troubleshooting, {compare.atlas-l.atlas-m.overall.task.trouble.difference|abs} points behind Atlas-L, also the costliest task to serve. The pass-or-fail judges are unnamed, and the cheaper models' lapses rest on them.
The owner declares a price per point of overall quality and floors on declining speculation, confirming account changes and unsupported claims; then the frontier below names one option.

claims.text: A point of overall quality costs {price.atlas-m.atlas-l.overall.per_point} per thousand conversations on the step from Atlas-M to Atlas-L, against {price.brisk-s.atlas-m.overall.per_point} on the step from Brisk-S to Atlas-M; Open-70B is the best buy at no price.

evidence.caption: Each step along the price frontier on overall quality, pooled over tasks by traffic share, with the price per point read off the gain's unpaired interval.

claims.text: Brisk-S and Open-70B trail both Atlas models on declining speculation, confirming before account changes and avoiding unsupported claims, each with an interval clear of Atlas-M's; the widest lapses reach {compare.atlas-m.brisk-s.declines.task.specul.difference|abs} points.

evidence.caption: Each model's pass rate on the policy behaviours, in the task that tests each, with intervals; the judge behind these rates is unnamed.

claims.text: Atlas-L scores higher than Atlas-M on overall quality in every task but speculation bait, most in troubleshooting at {compare.atlas-l.atlas-m.overall.task.trouble.difference|abs} points.

evidence.caption: Atlas-L less Atlas-M on overall quality in each task, with unpaired intervals.

claims.text: On every behaviour judged pass or fail, Atlas-M is not told apart from Atlas-L: each pair of intervals overlaps.

evidence.caption: Atlas-L and Atlas-M on each pass-or-fail behaviour, in the task that tests it, with intervals.

claims.text: Every model meets the {aspects.overall.bar.latency_s.atlas-l.bar} latency bar in every task; Atlas-L is the slowest, its tail reaching {task.research.atlas-l.latency_s.p95} on research questions.

evidence.caption: Latency per model and task, each bar from the median to the tail percentile.

explore.control: Price of a point of overall quality, per thousand conversations
explore.binds: Which measured option is the best buy
explore.outcome: Below {price.brisk-s.atlas-m.overall.per_point_low_unpaired}, Brisk-S; from {price.brisk-s.atlas-m.overall.per_point_high_unpaired} to {price.atlas-m.atlas-l.overall.per_point_low_unpaired}, Atlas-M; above {price.atlas-m.atlas-l.overall.per_point_high_unpaired}, Atlas-L. Inside each step's own band this run does not settle the pick, and Open-70B is the pick at no price.

explore.control: Whether the policy behaviours are guardrails
explore.binds: Whether Brisk-S and Open-70B stay in the trade
explore.outcome: With floors near the Atlas models' rates on declining speculation, confirming account changes and avoiding unsupported claims, both cheaper models drop out and the choice narrows to Atlas-M or Atlas-L.

omitted.what: Open-70B's persona small talk, where it reads highest on staying in character
omitted.why: Not told apart from either Atlas model there, and it lapses on the policy behaviours elsewhere; it changes no option a decider would weigh.

omitted.what: The cheaper models' rates on resolving troubleshooting issues, clear steps, escalation, tool calls and citations
omitted.why: They trail the Atlas models on these too; the policy behaviours already carry the case against them, and the full figures sit in the appendix.
The cost order is the same in every task; the pooled price frontier carries it.

omitted.what: Brisk-S against Open-70B, task by task
omitted.why: Mixed by task, and Open-70B is never the best buy at any price, so the comparison does not move the trade.
The snapshot keeps no failed trials to show.

next.text: The concierge owner declares a price per point of overall quality, per thousand conversations, and floors on declining speculation, confirming account changes and unsupported claims.
next.settles: Turns the tradeoff into a decision: the frontier then names one option.

next.text: Run a routed mix on the same cases: Atlas-L on troubleshooting, where its lead over Atlas-M is largest, and Atlas-M elsewhere.
next.settles: What such a mix keeps of Atlas-L's quality and Atlas-M's saving, so it can be priced beside the measured options.

next.text: Name the judge behind the pass-or-fail behaviours and calibrate it against human ratings, as the overall-quality judge was.
next.settles: Whether the cheaper models' policy lapses, and Atlas-M's parity with Atlas-L, hold under a trusted judge.

next.text: Declare the monthly volume of conversations.
next.settles: Turns each price per point into a monthly figure the owner can weigh against a budget.

method.text: {scoreboard.atlas-l.cases} conversations per model across the tasks, the same count for every model; no repeats are stated. No trial was lost ({scoreboard.atlas-l.lost} for Atlas-L, and likewise for the others).

An ordinal judged score per task, from a judge calibrated on {judged.overall.calibration_ratings} human ratings with {judged.overall.agreement} agreement. Overall figures pool the tasks, weighted by each task's traffic share as the input states it.
Each judged pass or fail in the one task that tests it. Nothing states whose judgement these are or how well it agrees with people.

Intervals at the level each table prints, per task and uncorrected. No model is a control and no paired contrast is stated, so every gap between two models combines their own intervals as if they ran different cases, which reads wider than a paired interval.
Cost per thousand conversations as stated per model, read as exact: no interval and no count of trials reporting it. No monthly volume is declared, so no monthly figure is given.
Median and tail percentile per task, against a {aspects.overall.bar.latency_s.atlas-l.bar} bar every model meets.
No gate, floor, margin or price per point was declared; the policy behaviours are read here as what a concierge must not get wrong, which is our reading, not a rule.

findings.finding: The sentence says Open-70B is the best buy at no price, but the block draws only the Brisk-S → Atlas-M and Atlas-M → Atlas-L steps. Add Open-70B's two per-point prices: $6.96 from Brisk-S (price.brisk-s.open-70b.overall.per_point) and $4.58 on to Atlas-M (price.open-70b.atlas-m.overall.per_point). Those numbers show why it is passed over at every price. If you'd rather not add them, drop the Open-70B clause from the claim.

The caption says each row is Atlas-L less Atlas-M 'overall and in each place', but the block has only the five task rows. Add the pooled row (+2.96, interval +1.98 to +3.94, from price.atlas-m.atlas-l.overall.gain_interval_unpaired) so the headline's gap sits next to its task breakdown. Otherwise, take 'overall' out of the caption.

The claim and Method both measure latency against 'the 9 s latency bar', but the snapshot declares no criterion of any kind, and Method says nothing was declared. A reader will take 9 s for a declared requirement. Say where 9 s comes from and label it as such (for example 'a 9 s line we chose, not a declared bar'), or state latency descriptively. Atlas-L's p95 tops out at 4.86 s on research questions, against 2.84 s for Atlas-M.

Fix the first confidence bullet: 'values a point of overall quality above $11.09 … moves the pick off Atlas-M' contradicts the decision block, which says the run doesn't settle the pick between $11.09 and $22.05. Write it as 'above $11.09 the pick is unsettled, and above $22.05 it moves to Atlas-L'. Separately, the confidence line says 'High' while the exclusion of the cheaper models rests entirely on pass-or-fail rates from an undescribed judge, and that caveat is missing from the confidence bullets. Add it there, or lower the stated confidence.

In the lean, 'It holds every policy behaviour at Atlas-L's level' claims more than atlas-parity shows, which is only that the two can't be told apart. Each difference interval still allows a gap of about 3 points (on confirming account changes, -2.8 to +2.8). Reword to 'is not told apart from Atlas-L on any policy behaviour'.

Widen the routed-mix next step. In persona small talk, Open-70B can't be told apart from Atlas-M on overall quality (90 against 88, difference -0.1 to +4.1). It has the highest staying-in-character rate (97%), costs $6.40 against $17.00 per thousand there, and that task tests no policy behaviour. Add Open-70B on persona small talk as a route to price beside Atlas-L on troubleshooting. Also revise the omitted-item reason that says it 'changes no option a decider would weigh'.

items.name: First screen
items.reason: The headline gives the trade: Atlas-L is 2.96 points higher on overall quality at 2.4 times the cost, and the two cheaper models lapse on policy. The decision block gives the lean (Atlas-M), the two prices where the answer flips ($11.09 and $22.05 per point, matching price.atlas-m.atlas-l.overall.per_point_low_unpaired and _high_unpaired), the main risk (the unnamed pass-or-fail judge) and who makes the call. The first claim, price-frontier, prices both steps. One snag: the first confidence bullet says a point worth more than $11.09 'moves the pick off Atlas-M', but the decision block says the run doesn't settle the pick between $11.09 and $22.05.

items.name: Coherent story
items.reason: Each claim matches its values table row by row. In atlas-l-lead, Atlas-L's lead is clear of zero in four tasks, and the speculation bait interval (-1.5 to +3.5) is the stated exception. In cheap-lapses, every cheaper-model interval sits clear of Atlas-M's: Brisk-S on declining speculation is 17 points behind (interval +10.3 to +23.7), and Open-70B on confirming account changes is 81% against 98%. In atlas-parity every Atlas pair overlaps. The pooled frontier (84.7, 89.83, 92.79) reproduces both step prices and puts Open-70B off the frontier. Nothing contradicts the headline.

items.name: Honest emphasis
items.reason: Atlas-M's quality gap to Atlas-L, its weakest task (troubleshooting, -5) and Atlas-L's slower tail all show. But the confidence is 'High' while the lean rests on things nothing declared: a price per point, policy floors that don't exist, and pass-or-fail rates from an undescribed judge. The judge caveat appears in Watch but not in the confidence bullets. The lean also says Atlas-M 'holds every policy behaviour at Atlas-L's level'. What atlas-parity actually shows is 'not told apart'. For example, on confirming account changes the Atlas-L minus Atlas-M interval runs from -2.8 to +2.8 points, so a shortfall of up to about 3 points is not ruled out.

items.name: Sound elision
items.reason: No omission changes the pick among the measured options. Open-70B is off the frontier (a point from Brisk-S to Open-70B costs $6.96; from Open-70B to Atlas-M, $4.58), and the cheaper models' other behaviours trail too. One omission does bear on the routed-mix next step. In persona small talk Open-70B's overall quality is 90, against 88 for Atlas-M (difference -0.1 to +4.1) and 91 for Atlas-L. Its staying-in-character rate is the highest of the four, at 97%. It costs $6.40 per thousand there, against $17.00 for Atlas-M. And no policy behaviour is tested in that task. So the reason given ('it lapses elsewhere') doesn't rule it out as a route.

items.name: Confounds handled
items.reason: Four confounds are each carried. No control: every interval is read unpaired, and the page says pairing would narrow intervals rather than reverse a direction. The undescribed judge: flagged on cheap-lapses and atlas-parity, named in Watch, and given a next step to calibrate it. Nothing declared: the lean is labelled as the analyst's own, with a declaration as the next step. Best of several candidates: stated with its direction. The 9 s latency bar is a separate problem, under item 7.

items.name: Actionable next steps
items.reason: Each step names an action and what it would settle. Declaring a price per point plus floors makes the frontier name one option. A routed mix, run on the same cases, prices a mix nobody has measured. Calibrating the pass-or-fail judge tests whether the lapses and the parity hold. Declaring monthly volume turns per-point prices into a budget figure.

items.name: Evidence fits claims

The latency claim and Method cite a '9 s latency bar', but the snapshot declares no criterion at all, and Method itself says nothing was declared.
